correctness.rationale: Berger's finite-emergence theorem supplies N distinct almost-everywhere empirical limits and positive basin weights, and the quantization characterization identifies metric emergence with minimum average distance to a finite prototype set. For any N-1 centers, assigning each of the N atoms to a nearest center forces two atoms i,j to share one center c; their weighted contribution is at least \(\min(p_i,p_j)(d_i(c)+d_j(c))\ge\min(p_i,p_j)d_W(\nu_i,\nu_j)\ge\Delta\). Conversely, remove the lighter atom of a pair attaining Delta and retain every other atom as a center; the cost is at most Delta. Hence the optimal N-1 distortion is exactly Delta. The source's strict error convention then gives equality N at epsilon=Delta and a drop for every epsilon>Delta. The argument allows arbitrary centers, not only empirical atoms.

final_claim:
If Berger's second metric emergence has finite small-scale value \(N\ge2\), with empirical-limit atoms \(
u_i\) of basin weights \(p_i\), then the first drop below N prototypes occurs exactly at \(\Delta=\min_{i<j}\min(p_i,p_j)d_W(
u_i,
u_j)\): both metric emergences equal N for \(0<\varepsilon\le\Delta\) and are at most N-1 for \(\varepsilon>\Delta\).
limitations: Only the first drop from N to fewer than N prototypes.
No assertion that the value is exactly N-1 for all larger resolutions.
